tweets.text:
Unofficially built myself 'Gemini Code' so I can try out Gemini 2.5 Pro like Claude Code. 

Some learnings:
→ I used Gemini 2.5 Pro in AI Studio to help me build it. I was in 'lazy Saturday' mode and gave very curt, non-descriptive tasks and it did fairly well without too much instruction BUT

→ As the project got more complex, it kept making the SAME syntax error, and at one point it said all we could do was pray (I laughed, it was worth it).

→ I've always been annoyed by function calling in Gemini, and the first way I was trying was yielding atrocious results (including Gemini's own prescribed path) but in the process I came up with a slightly different way of implementing a CLI assistant. Fun, definitely cool to try to 'rebuild' Claude code with a diff model. Interestingly, Gemini didn't think it would work at first when we were brainstorming solutions.

→ Because I'm throttled on requests per day (it's like 25-100 between free and tier 1), I needed to build a model picker inside the experience. Need to automate switching and maybe just tell the user subtly.

→ Working on some quality of life updates (like right now it's pretty rogue, need to build more human in the loop stuff) and then will release on Monday so others can use it too

tweets.text:
Try out Gemini Code: a coding assistant in your terminal powered by Gemini 2.5 Pro. 
💜 https://t.co/enhDbSVNmy 💜

Release Notes:
→ It's easy to get started, just run `pip install gemini-code` in a virtual environment, and then run `gemini` to initialize it. It requires your own API key, so don't forget to get one from https://t.co/8CKE51Jlqc 

→ I built this because I love Claude Code and wanted a similar experience -- I like that I can just use my own API key and Gemini is generally way cheaper as well. 

→ Found a bug? Feel free to fork the code and fix it (lol)! If you want to try to improve it, please do so - repo is public!

→ Reminder and a disclaimer that I don't work at Google and this is not an official Google project - just a weekend side hack 

→ It is highly likely you'll get throttled by rate limits - I put as much info as I can in the guide so you know what behavior to expect when that happens. You can also set which default model to use if you want to switch to 1.5 Pro.

tweets.text:
Camille Claudel: The Story of a Forgotten Artist

Camille Claudel (1864–1943) was a talented French sculptor, but for a long time, the world forgot her. Her story is a painful example of art, love, and society’s cruelty.

A Dream to Become an Artist

From childhood, Camille had an interest in sculpture. However, in the 19th century, women did not have easy access to art education. At that time, the famous École des Beaux-Arts in Paris was open only to men. Yet, she did not give up and enrolled in studios where women were allowed to learn.

Auguste Rodin and the Tragedy of Love

During her studies, she met the renowned sculptor Auguste Rodin. Their relationship was not just romantic but also a remarkable artistic collaboration. They created several sculptures together, some of which are now displayed in the Rodin Museum and Musée d'Orsay.

However, Rodin was already in a relationship with another woman. A few years later, he left Camille. This not only affected her personal life but also her career. Society rejected her—not just as Rodin’s lover but also as an artist.

Depression, Mental Hospital, and Struggles

Camille’s life became increasingly difficult. She fell into depression, and her sculptures stopped selling. Her brother, Paul Claudel, a famous poet and diplomat, did not help her either. Instead, considering her a "disgrace to the family," he had her forcibly admitted to a mental hospital in 1913.

Camille remained in the asylum for thirty years. She wrote many emotional letters, but no one came to her aid.

From Oblivion to Immortality

In 1943, Camille Claudel passed away. No family member attended her funeral, and she was buried in an unmarked grave.

However, over time, her art was rediscovered. Today, her sculptures are displayed in museums around the world. A museum dedicated to her, the Camille Claudel Museum, has also been established near Paris.

Conclusion

Camille Claudel’s story is not just that of an artist but also of struggle and identity. She was forgotten once, but today, she is remembered as a great sculptor. Her art and her perseverance continue to inspire future generations.
